Quick Dollar Drawdown Estimator (2000–2025 Historical Data)

Savers comparing the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) with the S&P 500 (SPY) usually look at a five-year return chart and stop there. A 25-year window tells a sharper story: semiconductor cycles compound rapidly during capital-spending waves, yet suffer deep multi-year declines whenever inventory gluts or interest-rate shocks hit.

In the 2000–2002 downturn, holding semiconductors alone meant watching $500,000 shrink near $127,000 and waiting more than seven years just to break even. The S&P 500 itself dropped 50.9% in 2008–2009 and needed 56 months to reclaim its prior peak.

Pairing SMH with non-cyclical US healthcare (XLV) and a short-term Treasury liquidity bucket (SGOV) behaved differently across all three historic stress periods. Because hospital demand, prescription volume, and medical devices rarely track chip factory cycles, semi-annual ratio resets mechanically shifted gains into ballast during booms and reduced drawdown depth during contractions.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did SMH take 89 months to recover after 2000 while SMH x XLV recovered in 17 months?

During 2000–2002, healthcare earnings held steady while semiconductor valuations compressed over 70%. Holding defensive XLV shares and rebalancing on a fixed calendar shortened the break-even timeline dramatically in historical data.

Does this comparison assume leverage or active daily trading?

No. Every series in Table I reflects unleveraged 1x spot index and ETF history with calm semi-annual ratio resets, published strictly for educational research.

How does SPY compare when a household is within five years of retirement?

SPY still suffered a 50.9% peak-to-trough drop in 2008–2009. Households drawing living expenses during a 50% slide face permanent capital depletion unless a defensive and Treasury cushion absorbs withdrawals.
